utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, and Jason Antley for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there are now housekeeping or preliminary matters that need detain us, may the usher escort the witness back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Kovacevic. Before counsel --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... resumes cross-examination, I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When my colleague Mr. Zecevic asked you about the powers and jurisdiction of the Military Prosecutor's Office regarding crimes against humanity, you gave a few very precise answers last Friday. I'd just like to go through certain parts of the same document you discussed with Mr. Zecevic, but it won't take long. I just want to put the position of the Defence regarding jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up P1284.10 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the document you discussed with Mr. Zecevic. These are guide-lines for identifying criteria for criminal prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment, please, I forgot my glasses. They are back in that -- reading glasses, yes, in the little bag. I'm really sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We thank Mr. Cvijetic while we wait for your eyeglasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3 of this document, please, in Serbian, and the same page in English. Page 3 in Serbian. One page further. This page is number two. We need the next page in B/C/S. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacevic, in item 3, we see that that Military Prosecutor's Office, in its instructive analysis of various types of crimes that would be under their jurisdiction, lists, under number 3, crime against humanity and international law from chapter 16 of the Criminal Code. That's where these crimes are listed and numbered; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On page 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In this instructive analysis, the Military Prosecutor's Office describes certain circumstances that have been observed in the units of the Army of Republika Srpska and explains how one should go about prevention. On page 4, at the end of the last paragraph - I'll quote it - they say: "In view of that, concerning crimes that occur from the conduct of persons in a situation of immediate threat of war, serious penalties, including the death sentence, are envisaged." You know that the state of immediate threat of war affects the sanctioning policy and the -- the prosecution policy?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We have to pause for a second between questions and answers so that the interpreters can follow and that the record be clear. As professionals, and, you, as a witness of that time, we know -- rather, I put it to you that regardless of whether the immediate threat of war had been declared or not, and that has political implications as well, de facto, from 1992 until 1995 in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was a permanent armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We also see, slightly above this passage that I quoted, a sentence where the Military Prosecutor's Office notes the following. It begins with the words: "Upon the proclamation of an imminent threat of war," and the year is 1993 [as interpreted], a general mobilisation had been declared. You know that all military conscripts had their wartime assignment and a work obligation during the armed conflict --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one correction to the transcript: Part of my question related to year "1992," not "1993," as was recorded on page 4, line 6. Can we move to page 12 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To my previous question recorded on page 4, line 3, the question was: During that generally mobilisation in 1992, all military conscripts had a certain wartime assignment and there was also a work obligation for those who did not have a wartime assignment to be involved in combat operations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If we look at page 12 of this instruction from the Military Prosecutor's Office, we see that they analyse certain elements of crimes, and in paragraph 2, we see that they say - and the sentence begins: "The greatest numbers of these crimes can be committed only in a time of armed conflict or they are, in some other way, closely related to armed struggle which requires that such crimes are committed as part of a large-scale military operation and on the orders of superiors." Now, I'm asking you as a former prosecutor, do you agree with this qualification, this legal qualification, of this group of crimes?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Further, the Military Prosecutor's Office, in their instructive analysis, towards the bottom of page 12, list one by one which acts constitute such crimes, and they qualify it as criminal and inhumane acts against the civilian population and prisoners of war, killings, torture, and inhumane treatment, rapes, establishment of camps, detentioning camps, looting property, and forced transfer of population. Unfortunately, very ugly things happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina and perpetrators were to be found among all the three ethnic groups. But what I'm interested in is this: A whole series of these acts listed in this analysis made by the Military Prosecutor's Office, we must say regrettably, although we learnt about it only later from the documents of -- and judgements of this Tribunal, happened also in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On page 14 of this instructive analysis, we see that the prosecutor is issuing a warning to the military commands and their staff. In paragraph 2, on page 14, the Military Prosecutor's Office cautions the Military Command Staff of the VRS about the following. And it all goes along the lines of well known rules from the times of the JNA, and it's all in line with the international humanitarian law. So, in paragraph 2, they say: "The very knowledge in possession of the Command Staff that units of the armed forces of the Army of Republika Srpska or their members committed or are committing such acts without any measures taken to redress the consequences or prevent the act, while subjecting the perpetrators to criminal prosecution, constitute liability for some of these criminal acts." Is that written there?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, in the next paragraph, the last sentence, reflects another instruction, namely, that military commands must inform the Military Prosecutor's Office of such occurrences. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in conclusion, on pages 15 and 16, the Military Prosecutor's Office gives a very precise order to unit commands related to detection of war crimes. And towards the bottom of page 15, you see that the command of the Main Staff demands precise reporting from all units on the ground; and, in fact, the Military Prosecutor's Office instructs units on the ground to work on detecting all cases of war crimes against humanity and war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This sentence is very important: "In the area of their responsibility." It is unequivocal here that a specific military commander, in the area of responsibility of his unit, must work to detect war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the lines that follow, the Military Prosecutor's Office very precisely instructs military commanders in their areas of responsibility to inform the nearest military authorities - military police, military judicial organs, et cetera - they instruct them to secure the crime scene, to ensure that evidence is collected by taking witness statements, preparing documentation, et cetera, et cetera. And in point 4, the military police and military judicial organs are instructed to give priority to these crimes in their work. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, who are the addressees of this instruction? We see on the next pages that it's made available to all the units, secretariats for national defence in all municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let's move to page 17; that's the final part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's also sent to police stations, the military police, military courts, et cetera. So to conclude, Mr. Kovacevic, it was not in dispute at all that the Military Prosecutor's Office had jurisdiction in 1992 and was in charge of prosecuting war crimes and crimes against humanity?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And it's not in dispute that all commanders of military units were duty-bound, in keeping with this instruction, to work on detecting and documenting any and all cases of violation of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you and your superiors in the Military Prosecutor's Office had contacts with the military judicial organs, where you harmonised your positions as professionals and dealt with issues of jurisdiction, if there were issues of jurisdiction between military prosecutions and civilian prosecutions.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To shed some more light on these activities, I'd like to call up P1285. It's a Prosecution Exhibit that relates to the work of the Military Prosecutor's Office. These are monthly reports, and we are not going to waste time on all of them. I'd just like to look at the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps because they cover the area of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could look at page 3 of this document, although it's marked 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's a monthly report, and the soldiers are very precise in their reporting. These are the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps. We see that the army filed one criminal report against a civilian for crimes against international humanitarian law. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You cannot know, of course, why -- why this criminal complaint was filed against a civilian, but we will see on page 13 of this monthly report what it was about. Let's just wait for that page to come up. So acting precisely with the instructions and the positions taken, the Military Prosecutor Office attached to the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps Command, the prosecutor is submitting, on page 13 - we can see this is under 8 - crimes against humanity, and we see that the Military Prosecutor Office has filed a criminal report against a certain Jozo Baric, pursuant to Article 142, for the massacre committed against members of the Serbian ethnic group on 17th of September in the village of Serdari. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you remember these events. These were turbulent times in September. You remember this event in which Serbs from the village of Serdari were killed, among them were even children and some elderly people as well?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that incident. There were, in fact, several similar incidents in which there was mass killing of the Serbian population in Kotor Varos municipality. And I remember this particular incident because this involved an extremely large number of victims and that among them were really small children. And I would just like to say one thing more and that is that in Kotor Varos, as a boarding municipality compared to Banja Luka municipality, in 1992 there were really many incidents of this nature, but I believe that this one involved the highest number of civilians killed by members of the Croatian -- or, rather, Muslim army. And for that reason it remained etched in my memory, and I remember it quite well at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Further on, on page 14, the Military Prosecutor's Office of the 1st and 2nd Corps, under chapter 4, it says that meetings were held with civilian organs in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the names of the places slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Derventa, Teslic, Knezevo, Laktasi, and Banja Luka. Considering the activities of the prosecutor's office, we are particularly interested in the fact that, among other things, in paragraph 3 of this chapter 4, it is focussed on contact with the judiciary, as we can see, in Derventa, Teslic, Knezevo - and Knezevo is, in fact, Skender Vakuf - and finally Laktasi and Banja Luka. In your contacts with your counterparts, did you acquire information that such communication existed between the Military Prosecutor's Office and members of the civilian judiciary in these area? Was there any exchange of information?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such meetings in 1992 and in later years, in 1993, for example. Yes, we had meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Further on, the Military Prosecutor's Office, as we can see, plans to establish active contacts with other civilian judiciary organs. And on page 19 - and then we shall finish with this document - we see that this report -- we are waiting for page 17 to come up on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 17, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We can see that this report was also submitted to the high prosecutor's office in Banja Luka. Correct me if I'm wrong, but, at that time, I presume that that refers to the district court -- or, rather, the district prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We do understand each other, but I'm asking you for the sake of the correction in the English transcript, where, under item 6, there is a question mark. So we want this to be clarified in the English version. So we are talking here about the district prosecutor's office who had jurisdiction at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, let's wrap up this subject and finalise the issue regarding the jurisdiction of the Military Prosecutor's Office, although our learned friends from the OTP are trying to fight very hard to prove otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, Your Honours, that's not really necessary. It's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If -- I do apologise. If you think that it's not at issue that military authority -- military judicial authorities were -- were under the -- the road to persecute war crimes committed by civilians, then I will not really -- if it's not in dispute between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the issue is with regard to the form of the question. I don't think it's appropriate for Defence counsel to be putting to the witness what or what isn't the Prosecution's position on a particular issue. He should just simply ask a question and get an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'll do that. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let us look and analyse document 65 ter 10293. And with this, we shall conclude this subject. However, we have to go through this document because that's also an integral part of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we leave this subject, I have a couple of questions that I might as well pose now in order to get the context right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly. I do apologise. I just have one question in relation to that and then you will have the floor, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Kovacevic, what we see here is a report by the prosecutor attached to the Main Staff of the army. I'm not going to speculate, but I think that this is a historic document issued by the prosecutor office because we heard from several testimonies that this was in the process of being established, but based on the number in the top right corner, which is number 1, and the date is the 9th of September, 1992, I conclude - and the author is Supic, the place is Han Pijesak, the date is 9 September 1992, where the prosecutor's office --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can move to page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This particular prosecutor's office, on the 26th of August, 1992, is instructing all the subordinate military prosecutor's office to give priority to prosecutions of crimes; for example, under bullet 3, where it says "against humanity and international law." So, Mr. Kovacevic, after all these documents, one can see the very clear responsibility and obligation on the part of military structures that whenever they learned that a crime against humanity was committed, they were duty-bound to prosecute, to collect evidence, and to carry out all other activities?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've finished with this line and with this topic, so if you have questions, of course, for ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I do apologise. Because it's 65 ter, I would like to ask to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: 65 ter number what?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D107, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. Mr. Kovacevic, I have a question that relates to the answer you gave to Counsel Pantelic when he was asking you whether you, as the public prosecutor, co-ordinated the efforts to investigate crimes with the military prosecutor on. On the rolling text on the screens in front of us, it's just at the turn between page 7 and page 8, and the question put to you was the following: "I suppose that you and your superiors in the Military Prosecutor's Office had contacts with the military judiciary organs, where you harmonised your positions as professionals and dealt with issues of jurisdiction ..." And then your answer was: "Yes, we had such meetings." My question to you goes to the nature of these meetings because, you see, the Chamber sits back with information provided to us by a number of witnesses that, in fact, a number of crimes were committed during the armed conflicts, as Counsel Pantelic says, by all three parties. Yet there has been, throughout this trial, an issue of which prosecutor should take the responsibility to have these crimes investigated and prosecuted; should it be the military prosecutor, or should it be the public prosecutor? And I think it is probably safe to say that a number of crimes that were in fact committed were never investigated or prosecuted by any of the two authorities of prosecution. So that brings me back to your answer. When you said that you had such meetings in which the public prosecutor and the military prosecutor would meet up and coordinate issues of jurisdiction, can you tell us about these meetings? How frequent did they take place? What were they about? And what were the actions taken, facing the reports that you received about the commission of crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in response to your question, I can give you the following answer: The public prosecutor represents the prosecutor's office. In other words, Nebojsa Pantic, the public prosecutor, represented the prosecutor's office in these and similar meetings. Just like, in such meetings, the district prosecutor's office of Banja Luka was represented by Milan Puvacic, the district prosecutor. I had an opportunity to attend, in 1993, I think, perhaps one of those meetings, along with the Prosecutor Pantic and the Prosecutor Puvacic, where a small number of criminal reports received were being discussed; that is to say, received by the Military Prosecutor's Office. These reports referred to -- or, rather, the discussion referred to the jurisdiction, whether it should be under the military or the civilian organs. In all these criminal reports that were the subject of this meeting, the offence cited was abscondment from the military forces, or theft of property of the military. And the perpetrators were reserve soldiers and civilians, in a number of cases. Therefore, a question was raised at this meeting of establishing subject-matter jurisdiction for these particular criminal reports and these particular criminal offences, given that the persons reported had changed their status; in other words, they were no longer reserve soldiers but became civilians in the meantime. That is to say, they were given a work obligation. And in the instances where civilians were the perpetrators of crimes within the domain of general crimes against military property, these civilians had left Republika Srpska or, rather, the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That meeting, as far as I could conclude and from what I knew, there was no dilemma in anyone's mind that the military prosecutorial authorities had jurisdiction for crimes against the civilian population and the international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacevic, for this clarification. Now, if I understand your testimony correctly, the jurisdiction between -- or, rather, the division of jurisdiction between military and public prosecutors would also depend on the status of the perpetrator; is that correct? I'm asking you this because you testified just a while ago that the status of the perpetrator had changed. As long as he was a reservist, he would fall under the jurisdiction of the military prosecutors; but if he changed his status and became a civilian, then he would come under the public prosecutor's office. Was that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were the topics that we had to discuss to harmonise our positions between the Military Prosecutor's Office and civilian prosecutor's offices. They had to arrive at a common position regarding jurisdiction over civilians who had to be prosecuted for such offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. How would, for instance, a murder committed against a civilian during the armed conflict be handled? Would that be handled as a war crime or as a private crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only speak about common practice. In determining jurisdiction in 1992, and that continued throughout the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, if there was a murder or a multiple murder, according to common practice with regard to civilian perpetrators, criminal reports were filed by police authorities. And the crime, if it involved several victims, would be qualified as murder from Article 36, it would be aggravated murder - Article 36, para 2, I believe - and, as such, it was to be prosecuted by the civilian prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wish to be very clear about this because you seem to be saying that the jurisdiction really depended on the status of the perpetrator. So, in other words, the military prosecutor would assume jurisdiction over a murder as a war crime only if the perpetrator belonged to the armed forces, either as a regular combatant or as a reservist. Is this correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about the actual practice of military prosecutor's offices regarding prosecutions from this chapter, chapter 16 of the Criminal Code. My knowledge about jurisdiction for prosecuting crimes in the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the duration of the conflict is what I just described. From what I know, both in the territory of Republika Srpska and in the territory of the Federation, the jurisdiction was the same in prosecutions of these crimes if - I repeat - these crimes were reported, Article 36, para 2, civilian authorities had jurisdiction; but in other cases, if somebody reported a crime against the civilian population or international law, such reports went directly to the Military Prosecutor's Office and the military authorities in the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. From what I know, that was the practice throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Kovacevic. I don't think I should be taking more of the Defence counsel's time, so I give the floor back to Mr. Pantelic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacevic, in your answers to my learned friend Mr. Olmsted and also the Defence team of Mr. Stanisic, you said that in our legal system that prevailed in 1992 there was a certain change in jurisdiction - I believe it was in June 1992 - when jurisdiction for practically all crimes was transferred from higher courts to lower courts, higher authorities to lower authorities.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I believe you may remember that at the same time jurisdiction over the work of the police was also adjusted. And we should look at P1090. While we're waiting: The principle was that there should be cooperation between the lower court, the lower prosecutor's office, and police stations in coordinating and detecting war crimes because of the change in jurisdiction that I just described?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You probably haven't seen this document before, and we didn't -- don't need to discuss it. But to illustrate this change of jurisdiction on the 2nd of July, 1992, a certain Mr. Josic, who was a police inspector in a public security station, head of the criminal investigations department, we see that policemen from Banja Luka are complaining to their superiors in the CSB Banja Luka, saying that they do not have enough staff to fight the amount of crime that is placed in their lap after this change of -- in jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbian, in e-court, we need page 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It was signed by Chief -- by the Chief Tutus, and the report was prepared by Mr. Josic. And it says: In view of the new obligations and the shortage of staff and the increased number of crimes that are now within our jurisdiction, et cetera, et cetera. What was the situation with the prosecutor's office? Did you encounter problems once a whole series of crimes were transferred to your jurisdiction? But very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many problems. A very extraordinary situation reigned in the whole of Banja Luka. The war started. There were no qualified staff, qualified officers. And such a huge inflow of cases was very difficult to prosecute within a reasonable amount of time. All of a sudden, we had dozens of cases a day received by the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We'll pause here. Mr. Kovacevic, you said it your statement to OTP investigators, and we heard it also from your colleagues who testified here, prosecutors and judges, there were many cases of attacks by army members against prosecutors and judges. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the prosecutors and judges in question are precisely those who did their work professionally and risked their lives sometimes because of that. Have you heard of that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did. I myself was in such a position a couple of times. My car was shot at. My apartment was shot at. It all happened in 1992. Once, in the courtroom, a civilian, or somebody from the audience because it was a public trial, set off an explosive device. We did not have any police in the courtroom. We didn't have qualified personnel who would conduct security checks before letting anyone come into the courtroom. It was very difficult for prosecutors to work in 1992 in every way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So if I understood correctly, in a trial where you were the trial attorney, armed individuals threatened your life, because, at that time, almost everyone carried arms.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm now specifically interested in the region of Prijedor. Of course, we can't analyse it all now, but in 1992, did you have any knowledge about Prijedor as a rather idiosyncratic region, political and other ways. There were rumours that certain officials from Prijedor were acting any way they liked. How was Prijedor treated within the Autonomous Region of Krajina? What was its reputation? What were the stories going around?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know of the Prijedor area, indeed, that area functioned in a different way than the rest of Krajina in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in view of certain structures, primarily in the police force, the situation was very difficult to control. It was very difficult to -- to get good information if something happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: There was a question from my learned friend Mr. Olmsted where you said you came up against a wall of silence in your own work, and you mentioned the example of Prijedor. The difficulties that you encountered as prosecutors, were they shared by other authorities that had to communicate with Prijedor? Did they also find it difficult to get information from Prijedor, to get anything that was necessary from Prijedor if it was necessary for prosecutions and detection of crimes?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I tried to say in my answer to the Prosecutor. Other authorities came up against a similar wall of silence in -- in getting information, in exchanging information with the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, please, Mr. Kovacevic, let us just note for the record that in Prijedor area there was a very strong and well-organised unit - I don't know of which level, whether it was a brigade or a tactical group - of the Army of Republika Srpska made up of military staff who were conducting combat operations on the front line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And, of course, in view of the instruction given by the prosecutor, it was only logical to expect the commanders, the army commanders and other commanding staff, to know what was going on in the area of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, now we have to conclude this cross-examination. And, for that purpose, we have to move to specific analyses of two crucial cases. The first one is the Koricanske Stijene crime. And the so-called Vrbas case -- or, rather, the non-Serb victims who were thrown into the Vrbas. Both these heinous and brutal crimes took place in August of 1992. First of all, you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that it is in line with the law -- the role of the prosecutor is to prosecute ex officio certain crimes and, among other things, to direct the preliminary criminal proceedings which is stipulated by the law. So, therefore, you will agree with me that the prosecutor plays a certain active role in insisting on the process of detecting the perpetrators and other things; of course, in cooperation with the police?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course, there is hierarchy within the prosecution's office. You said that Mr. Pantic was your boss, then Mr. Puvacic was his boss, and finally I think that it was Mr. Gladanac at the level of the republic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As we could see, both in the activities of public and military prosecutor offices, certain positions were taken towards the policy of prosecution, depending on different circumstances. And in that way, the prosecutor's role was that of an active agent in combatting crime in society. You accomplished that through certain directives and consultations at the level of the prosecutor's office and adopted strategies of how to proceed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, in our legal system, the investigating judge also had a certain active role to play. This is beyond dispute, and the Trial Chamber gathered as much from your answers. Now, can you please explain to the Trial Chamber, when you receive a criminal report against an unidentified perpetrator, you register the case and you propose certain things to the investigating judge. Now what I'm interested in is the following: Is the investigating judge autonomous in conducting this investigation? He is allowed to issue certain orders and carry out certain activities without your knowledge; or is he directly linked with your activity? Can you just explain this procedure briefly.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll just give you a short explanation: The investigating judge is an organ investigating the whole case. In any specific situation, or in the specific case of Koricanske Stijene, the investigating judge had commenced an on-site investigation. And as long as it lasts, and it can last indefinitely, but preferably should last as short as possible, but while it's ongoing, the investigating judge plays an absolutely independent and active role with regard to collecting all the information, taking statements from the individuals that might in any way provide valuable information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Will you stop there, please. So the investigating judge may carry out certain activities without even informing you as the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He doesn't have to give me prior notice, but he must inform me subsequently about the activities that he had carried -- he or she had carried out. He was entitled to carry out a series of activities, and then when -- the summary of all these activities, after a certain period, should be passed on to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And, of course, each and every participant in this part of the proceedings have their respective role under the law. The prosecutor is free to seek assistance from other state authorities, like the army, police, et cetera. There are no limitations in his attempt to gather evidence.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no limitations whatever. He can contact military security authorities. Particularly in this particular case, which, in view of the activities of the prosecutor's office, was very special - I'm talking about the Koricanske Stijene case - there was a dilemma whether we would have jurisdiction for the on-site investigation or whether that would be within the jurisdiction of the military authorities. Because we didn't know at the very beginning who the victims were. So he was obliged to coordinate his work, if necessary, with the military security organs and other military authorities, and he could do that autonomously.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that in these contacts with the military judiciary, the military distanced themselves from the whole case. They refused to undertake any measures. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That became quite apparent quite soon. Some 15 or 20 days later, we faced certain difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at Prosecution Exhibit -- yes -- well, this dispatch is part of P18567, but in order to be more efficient, can we -- can we please look P675.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Speaking of this subject, let us shed the light on the role of the military, specifically in those times when all the events were revealed very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please enlarge this for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We can see that the dispatch was sent on the 21st of August, 1992. It's an extraordinary operational report. And the commander of this area of responsibility, Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic says -- or, rather, proposes a committee to be formed within the Krajina Corps to carry out an on-site investigation. And at the end he proposes that the CSB organs be informed as well. So he is talking about a report of a mass killing taking place on that location. And in according with the instructions that Mr. Peulic received from the Military Prosecutor's Offices, practically proposing some other measures as well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic is a professional officer, very experienced, and he knows very well that if such a serious thing takes place in his area of responsibility, what should be done. Now, what I'm asking you is the following: In your opinion - and you are a professional - if we know that in this period, not all the details are yet available, whether the military was involved, whether the police was involved, what was the situation particularly in view of the jurisdiction for prosecuting crimes against civilians, tell me, did ever anyone from the military judiciary or military security authorities contact you or your boss, Pantic, seeking cooperation in detecting the perpetrators of the Koricanske Stijene crime? Did you have any cooperation in that sense at all?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know and remember, we did not have any cooperation on this particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now let's be very specific. In 1992, you couldn't have known to what extent the police was involved in certain detecting work. You have issued certain orders, but when you came here and you spoke to the OTP, you were shown a set of documents and correspondence, including dispatches, in which the chief of the Prijedor police informs the chief of the CSB that the individuals who are suspected of possibly committing these crimes are members of the military and are assigned the certain military tasks. Now I'm asking you, what was the obligation of the military prosecutor and the military security organ in light of the information that we see in this dispatch? What was the military prosecutor and the military security organs were supposed to take on the basis of the suspicion that the perpetrators were among their ranks?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least they should have taken a copy of this criminal report and carry out this part of the job, provided they establish that it's their jurisdiction at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that my learned friend Mr. Olmsted is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I was going to object to the form of the question which not only is it extremely long and complex but it's also misleading. The document we have in front of us states that the convoy of buses that went to Koricanske were escorted by members of the Prijedor and Sanski Most civilian police. And then later on it states that these police officers participated in the liquidation. And then it further states that the military units had nothing to do with this. So unless perhaps Mr. Pantelic is offering a hypothetical question - if the perpetrators happened to be military, should the Military Prosecutor's Office have done something about it - then, perhaps, that's a proper question. But here it's assuming facts not in evidence. And this witness, as he has testified, simply didn't get any information regarding who the perpetrators were, other than, of course, this particular memo from the military which states it was the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We would take the break now, and Mr. Pantelic would have the opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- rephrase that question when we return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, Mr. Pantelic, you will attempt your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Kovacevic, we see on the screen this interim report, a dispatch from the commander, Mr. Peulic. And Peulic uses qualifications very correctly. He says, in fact, genocide against civilians. He is not a lawyer. The word "genocide" was used by all the three sides for propaganda purposes. But it's indubitable that this concerns a very large number of the civilians, that it happened within the area of responsibility. And it's indubitable that according to the instruction previously received, commander Peulic is informing his superior command about this crime. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now let's go back to the line of questioning that we started before the break. Either it's a question of interpretation or a misunderstanding with Mr. Olmsted. I was not asking anything hypothetically. I will show you now the same documents that he has shown you before; namely, dispatches concerning communication between CSB Banja Luka and CSB Prijedor about where the members were, whether they were in the army or not, et cetera. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But before we get to that, we must - because you are a professional and so are the Judges here who will dispense justice - we are not having a trial against institutions or organisations. We have on trial, individuals who are being tried for individual responsibility. That's why I'm asking you: Did my client, Mr. Zupljanin, ever give you any orders to obstruct an investigation or did he advise you not to conduct an investigation? Did he ever obstruct justice?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information that my client, Mr. Zupljanin, ever, in relation to your superior, Mr. Pantic, excerpt any pressure, maybe Pantic complained to you that he was under pressure not to investigate or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any information that Mr. Zupljanin obstructed anything in this case, from what I know or from what Mr. Pantic told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In this area of individualising criminal responsibility, we have to explain to the Trial Chamber the structure of CSB Banja Luka and its work vis-à-vis the prosecution, and the specific tasks of individual people in prosecuting perpetrators of crimes. Now, let us look at a Prosecution Exhibit. P1567. It's a voluminous document related to criminal reports that have to do with KTN Koricanske Stijene and KTN Vrbas that we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, this is a document we'll have to analyse later. I'll need 2D71 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is, in fact, the Vrbas case, the killing of those non-Serbs and the bodies found in Vrbas. It's not a separate document; it's part of a case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we need page 16, if I'm not mistaken. Perfect, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Before we analyse further the work of the police and the prosecutor and the investigating judge, tell me: As an experienced prosecutor, you know what police work is, what a work-plan is, the operative work-plan when the police is working based on the instructions of the investigating judge or its own senior officials; it's a plan that says how they should conduct a specific operation?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: A very important issue is cooperation with --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is the right English version. But we need the second page in English with the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Kovacevic, you were a prosecutor for many years. You cooperated on daily activities with members CSB Banja Luka. The chief of the centre was Mr. Zupljanin; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Assistant chief and the chief of public security was Djuro Bulic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, under Djuro Bulic, there was a series of departments and sections, but we are now interested in the department for crime prevention. Below Djuro Bulic was the chief of the crime prevention department in CSB Banja Luka, and his name was Milorad Djuric; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, depending on the type of case and the number of cases, there was also in the hierarchy a chief of section for general crime prevention; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that was Zivko Bojic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then there was the leader of the team of inspectors. Nobody works alone but in a team. And that was the inspector from this general crime prevention section, and that was Mr. Dragomir Markovic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, when you, as a prosecutor from the basic prosecutor's office, have communication and cooperate with others, I assume - and you will correct me if I'm wrong - you are in charge of specific cases. And in certain operations, you communicate with Chief of Sector Bulic, or Chief of Section Bojic, or Section Chief Djuric and the operative team; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, it's different from your superior Mr. Pantic; he has the same communication with someone else at a different level of the CSB; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's very important here, Mr. Kovacevic, for the sake of establishing the truth, that Stojan Zupljanin is not a one-man orchestra and a magician with a wand. He has, under him, well-trained professionals in different departments whose job is to deal with certain types of crimes and carry out operative work.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now that we have noted all the players in a certain police operation, let us go back ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague advises me that we should later return to this work-plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the case of Koricanske Stijene. In your evidence given to the Prosecution, you also analysed certain documents and dispatches that are in the case file. For the record to be precise and to have the correct chronology, I will put to you certain dates and we will go through this chronology together. This serious crime occurred on the 21st of August, 1992, at Koricanske Stijene; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: CSB Banja Luka files a criminal report against an unidentified perpetrator on 8 September 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember your answer to the Prosecutor, you were in charge, because there is an certain procedure of registration through various organs of the prosecutor's office, and you were entrusted with the case. You received it on the 10th or 11th.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was officially received by the prosecutor's office on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The 11th of September?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: There is a letter where you propose to the investigating judge that certain investigative actions be taken, and the date of that letter to the investigating judge is the 14th of September, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge, after several witness interviews conducted at your proposal, believes that this particular action has been completed and returns the case to you on the 24th of September.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it here on the screen, but I believe it was the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And on the 30th of September, 1992, you issue an instruction to the members of the crime police in CSB Banja Luka to continue operative work to identify the perpetrators; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So we have here, roughly speaking, a month of exchange between various authorities; the prosecutor's office and the police. It all took place within a month and ended with your order to continue operative work.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you arrived here in The Hague, the OTP showed you some other dispatches between CSB Banja Luka and Prijedor regarding these operative actions. You said you did not remember that from 1992. You don't remember seeing it, but you were looking through them with the Prosecution. I'd like to go through those documents with you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, let us take P1573.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We'll start with this document. CSB Banja Luka is sending this dispatch to the SJB Prijedor quoting a dispatch from the MUP of Republika Srpska dated 31st August 1992 and gives orders to Prijedor to take written statements from the policemen who escorted the convoy, to provide the personal details of these police officers by the 15th of September. Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's an integral part of police work, isn't it, in efforts to identify the perpetrators; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the next document now. I'm sorry we can't have everything on the screen at the same time to see a whole overview.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next one is P682.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of September, 1992, SJB Prijedor sent a dispatch to SJB Banja Luka, and the reference is the request from 11 September, and the public security station of Prijedor says the following: 1, SJB Prijedor is unable to carry out an investigation into the incident at Koricanske Stijene. It's clear from this that CJB Banja Luka required an investigation and required certain steps to be taken by SJB Prijedor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think we have been through this already quite intensively. So unless you're able to bring something completely new to this, I suggest you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I was about to stand up, myself, because really these documents are with regard to internal workings of the RS MUP, and this witness was a prosecutor at the time. And so I don't know if there's even foundation for him to comment on communications between the CSB and Prijedor. They -- Mr. Pantelic certainly could ask whether this witness was aware of this information contained in this dispatch; but, beyond that, what more can he provide?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is very simple. We have four very important dispatches which I want to line up here for the record and for the final determination for the submission. This witness, was aware about a certain number of these dispatches during proofing with the OTP. So, I am not going to go into every detail. I just want to see and hear from this witness, in light of his professional experience as a prosecutor, where the military jurisdiction and military organs are fitted in this particular case of Koricanske Stijene. And I will show you just in a few moments how we see -- I mean, we shall ask from witness if can he give us some -- some answers and his personal knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that. Unless the four documents that you want to show to the witness are already on the record and unless the witness now offers some other answer to the question as to whether the military indicated right away its reluctance to investigate the Koricanske Stijene incidents. I think the witness gave a clear answer when he was confronted with the document in which Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic said that this was not anything of the military's business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If you want to respond, please do. I'll ask my question afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I would like to draw the attention of this Trial Chamber and to discuss this particular part from a witness that we have here in light of his previous prosecutor experience. What the further steps should be taken when the information of potential alleged perpetrators being a member of army should be done. That's -- that's the point, actually. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, yes, the Prosecution doesn't have a problem with that question as long as it's clear who should take those steps. If you're talking about what the Military Prosecutor's Office should do, again, this witness was with the civilian prosecutor's office, and those questions are best asked to someone who was with the Military Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I completely agree with you, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacevic, let us look at the next fact that seems to follow from this. We see that these persons, whose details are requested, were, as of 9 September, in the military units in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And we also see from this that upon the request of the army and the Red Cross, some order or request was finally issued for these police officers to be attached to this convoy.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, please tell the Court, in a situation like this, when potential perpetrators are in the ranks of the army, what can you as a prosecutor tell us? What kind of measures are to be taken by the military prosecutor or by you as the civilian prosecutor? Just hold on a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That question is misleading because this document does not say that these police officers were members of the military. It says they were sent to the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, let's disregard this objection because my learned friend should know that his own Exhibit P618 speaks by itself about who and where was sent and under which authority. So that's why I want to go through this particular documents because it's of the crucial importance for the Defence of my client, in terms of showing what the relevant departments of -- criminal department of CSB is doing in the meantime and also to see and to hear - if, of course, this witness is -- is able to give us the answer - what he as a civilian prosecutor in this particular case will -- will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- which measures. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, if I understand you well, you take it from this document that there is an indication that members of the military were among the perpetrators; is that right? Because that's what you're suggesting already two or three times. Is that -- is that what --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, we know that before September, before August, and after August, namely, on the -- on the 9th of September, we don't know upon which order and how members of a special platoon from Prijedor were sent to -- to the front and became, actually, military -- military officials. So that's the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So you're linking the Koricanske Stijene killings with policemen under resubordination on the basis of this document? That's -- that's one -- perhaps one of the documents, but this is one of the documents, in your view, that indicates that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, it's -- it's a misunderstanding. No, no. The position is the following, that from 9th of September 1992, there are ample evidence and lot of informations that members of who are in the -- in the -- in this convoy, members of SJB Prijedor, upon certain order were sent to military -- to military operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: After the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: After the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And your position is, because they are, at that moment, as Mr. Drljaca is saying, under the command of the military, it should be the military -- military jurisdiction investigating?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Like this, it's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let's move to document P -- I'm sorry I'm trying to put this in chronological order. This was a response from the 11th of September. Yes, that's the reply to this dispatch. Now we're coming to the next dispatch. CSB Banja Luka, 7th October 1992. It's Prosecution Exhibit 61 -- P617.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So another dispatch concerning Koricanske Stijene. Prijedor is required to provide a detailed answer. Which police officers escorted the convoy. 2, was there anyone else on the security detail. 3, what did these police officers write in their reports when they came back. And, 4, a report on the on-site investigation. And then identification and burial. You see the document?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that this was the usual practice of the police in the process of detecting the perpetrators, so this is a normal relationship that existed in that context?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, let's look at Prosecution Exhibit P618. And that's the last document in this set. So P618. Here it is. Can we please enlarge the document for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So, on the 13th of October, Prijedor replies to the CSB dispatch sent on the 7th of October by saying the following: That the individuals who had been escorting the convoy, members of the Prijedor SJB, were currently carrying out war assignments. And then they say that they had provided certain additional information, et cetera. Now, in the context of all these documents, tell me this: Number one, the case, KTN, was open, it was registered, and the police obliged -- is obliged to carry out their work constantly with a view to detecting the perpetrators; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Number two, it has been noted that the civilian police, in view of this information, has no competence over members of the military at that point in time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It has also been noted, and it is a fact, that this case would never be closed unless the individuals who are in the army come to the jurisdiction of the civilian police and be brought in subsequently. That's the normal procedure, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In your professional opinion, what would you, as a prosecutor, do in a situation like this? You have information that certain suspects are under the jurisdiction of the military. What would your task as a public prosecutor be in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, I would notify the military prosecutor, or I would even defer the report to the Military Prosecutor's Office. So I would resort to either of the two options.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me this: Since the military security organs, on the basis of dispatch sent by Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic, were aware of the incident -after all, it was published in international and local media - tell me, what is the role of the military prosecutor in this specific case as well as security organ, since they knew that the suspects from Prijedor were in the ranks of the army? What would their duty be under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military authorities should have done something which would be identical to the -- what would be done by the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In other words, the military authority knew what had happened, they knew that the potential suspects had been sent from Prijedor to Han Pijesak to join the military on someone's order. So what was the security organ of the army doing in that situation?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organ should temporarily arrest these individuals, put them in custody, and subsequently transport them as soon as possible to the military police. After operational processes of these suspects, they would be brought before the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But to follow up on this answer that you just gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Maybe you were proceeding to that same issue, I don't know. But, Mr. Pantelic, you looked as if you were moving on to something else. But before we do that, my question to you, Mr. Kovacevic, would be: If the military police would arrest some members of the armed forces who had just been resubordinated to the army but having committed the crime at Koricanske Stijene while they were still policemen and, thus, under the jurisdiction of the public prosecutor, would the military prosecutor then continue to prosecute and investigate, or, rather, the other way around, investigate and prosecute the perpetrators, since they were now under the army's jurisdiction; or would he refer them back to the public prosecutor, assuming that it would fall under the public prosecutor's jurisdiction since the crimes were committed at a time when the perpetrators were policemen? Can you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not at all simple to explain. In view of the fact that members of the police were also members of certain structures of the armed forces on the ground, what I want to say is that some of those individuals who were in the escort could have been, as per establishment and as a reserve police officer, a member of the military unit deployed somewhere on the front line. Under such circumstances, there is no doubt that it was -- it would be the military prosecutor who would have jurisdiction over such individuals, and there is no dilemma about that whatsoever. Therefore, the military prosecutor, in this particular instance, should establish the deployment, as per establishment, of each and every individual, or, rather, their assignment, prior to their being sent to carry out these military missions in and around Han Pijesak. Once they established that, then it is to be decided whether this particular perpetrator of the crime was a member of the armed forces as a reserve police officer and whether he was under the command of the military authority or not. So, the entire reserve police force, the special police units, and all other police structures - I mean individuals from these structures - could have been members, as per establishment, of combat units of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Could I just ask you directly if, to your knowledge, any attempt was made by the police to relieve the public prosecutor's office of jurisdiction over this crime by resubordinating and transferring the perpetrators from Koricanske Stijene to the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is difficult for me to speak, sir, about somebody else's decision taken within certain structures relating to sending someone to the battle-field in order, perhaps, to thwart the conduct of certain proceedings. That seems to be -- me to be highly unlikely. It is possible, but incredible. Because, under such circumstances, these individuals would be exposed to death or sustaining injuries. Therefore, I very much suspect that anyone would agree to that. He would rather flee from the army in order not to be sent to the zone of combat operations on the front line and, thus, avoid being killed or injured. They would try to find their way out of such a situation which, undoubtedly, could have led to their death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If I -- if I may, I have -- I have a question for the witness as well. But before that, I would like to be sure about the document that is referred to in the document on the screen, where it is said: We sent the information which you had requested for all the policemen who escorted that convoy in your document number 11-12-16 dated 26th of September, 1992. Do we know what that information was? Do we have that document? Does anyone, a public prosecutor or Defence knows -- know what information that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, you're referring to the 22 September 1992 dispatch that Chief Drljaca says he sent to the CSB? I do not believe we have that document. So we're -- we have to draw inferences from this particular dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We are in even a worse position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll ask my question anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... in the hands of OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I seem to remember that you said, I think during examination-in-chief, that you asked for the name of all the policemen who were escorting the convoy but that you never got that list. You never got a reply on that request. Is that right? Do I remember that well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you do. I'm sorry, Your Honours, I stand corrected. Not the policemen. I asked -- submitted a request for a checkup of individuals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, thank you. And, now, as you were asked a series of hypothetic questions, I would ask one -- I would add one to that. Here, it is said: "We hereby inform you that a policemen ... who escorted the convoy from Prijedor to Knezevo ... are at present on War Commissions [sic] ..." And this would then be the reason to hand over the jurisdiction on -- on these people to the military prosecutor. But wouldn't one expect or -- or request, anyhow, the names of those -- those people who were escorting -- the people who were escorting and the people, if any, who were resubordinated to the military, as information from somebody one knows that was involved in the Koricanske Stijene incident and that one could perhaps suspect of covering up or covering the perpetrators? Would you not have asked for those names and just be satisfied by the response, They're not longer here, they're somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is difficult for me to answer such a hypothetical question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Witness, you're --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you're answering hypothetical questions all the time, the last 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes, I apologise, Your Honours. Since I am expected to give my personal assessment of the situation, that is to say, whether the names of the perpetrators were known by someone who sent this letter to Mr. Simo Drljaca, and then Mr. Drljaca is responding in this manner. I don't know if this information was known to the seeker of the information. All I can do is to repeat what is stated herein, which says in line 3, second sentence: "In our document number 11-12-16, dated 22nd September, 1992 ..." We've lost the document. Now it's all right. "... we sent the information that you requested for all the policemen who escorted the convoy in question." And I honestly don't know whether all the information was provided, in order to be able to give a direct answer to your question. In the criminal, legal sense and for purposes of operative work, at least in our system, just a name and surname are not enough to identify a person. What I'm trying to say is that along with a name and surname, we need the mother's maiden name, date of birth, and all the personal details that are necessary to identify the perpetrator of a crime. All these details would be necessary for me to be able to say that whoever requested this information knew the identity of the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if this is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But by all means you confirm that all the information, although you asked for it as well, it was never provided to you, as a public prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. We did not receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us wrap up this topic. Members of the crime prevention service, or CSB Banja Luka in this correspondence with Prijedor, do not have any jurisdiction over military authorities and persons who are in the army. As far as they're concerned, this is an open case but they are unable to act?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, please tell the Trial Chamber: Who is authorised to send these people from Prijedor to Han Pijesak? Is it the police who would send them or is it the competent military unit that issues an order for transfer?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the competent military body is in charge of transferring a person to a military unit, to a certain position.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this witness is entitled to his opinions, but this -- this witness is not a member of the police. He is -- there's been no foundation laid that he would know anything about the policies of resubordination between the RS MUP and the VRS. But, obviously, he answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Oh, come on. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacevic, please, did you ever serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.
