utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have the rank of reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know, both as a prosecutor and as a man who has been through all these military structures, who and when orders an individual to be sent to a certain military position?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions on this topic. But I do have other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, look, please, at this series of events. First of all, in August 1992, this really heinous crime, you saw the documentation shown you by the Prosecutor. Then we have certain actions by the district prosecutor in Banja Luka in 1999. And, finally, trials before the BH state court in Sarajevo in 2008, 2009, and 2010, judgements included. This is the series of steps and actions in relation to Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Twenty years is the time it took to gather all the legal elements and take action, and you worked in a prosecutorial position at the time, with the proviso that at a certain point in your tenure, jurisdiction changed?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, as a professional and a man who lived this period, tell me, In 1992 and 1993 in this wartime turmoil, was it possible to take all this action that was ultimately taken seven years later in peacetime? Were you able to work in the same way, with the same results, in 1992 and 1993 as after the war?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very difficult to work in 1992 and 1993. It was not possible to achieve the same quality of work that we were able to achieve in peacetime, under normal circumstances. Such serious crimes with very grave consequences could hardly be expected to be dealt with quickly, with an efficient outcome, and that the perpetrates be brought to justice quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But we would agree that the operative officers in CSB Banja Luka, under the circumstances, did everything to document the crime, and created a basis for eventual closure of the case 18 years later?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's look -- let's look at P1567.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: While it's coming up, we have to deal with serious problems in documentation. You saw yourself that there are dispatches missing, elements are missing, and even parts of the case file are missing. First of all, tell the Trial Chamber when the case file was opened in the prosecutorial office, the KTN file? It has a cover, it has a folder.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's usually cardboard -- a cardboard folder?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had cover files, although it was not exactly cardboard. There were shortages of everything, including paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On the inside of this cover, there must be a list of every document put in, every enactment, every communication with anyone?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As a prosecutor, it's your responsibility and your duty to make a record of certain actions. You tell your assistants -- your assistants, Please put it in the agenda that we have to do this and this and this in November 1992. It's your duty?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the acronym for these actions by the court is EV, short for record.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. EV, or "skontro, [phoen]" SC.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And when you came here to testify, the Prosecution did not show you the folder of the file. They showed you some documents from the file, but the prosecutorial official file is -- the folder is something you haven't seen?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the basic prosecutor's office or the district one?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The basic one.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So we don't have that folder of the file opened in September 1992, and we can only guess what was in it and what wasn't in it. All that we were able to reconstruct was from the documents shown us by the Prosecutor; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now let's go to page 32 of this document to try to assist the Trial Chamber by explaining all the stages that Banja Luka went through in 1992 and 1993 that affected this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, we need the next page. The page after this. The ERN number ends in 497. Now, could we zoom in on the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Why is this document important? This is a document from 1999, where the chief of the CSB Banja Luka, Mr. Sutilovic, says in paragraph 3: "Due to the conditions and circumstances under which this centre worked at the time, especially the events related to the Operation Septembar 1993 and Hurricane, and several incursions by the SFOR into the centre who removed a lot of documentation from this centre, we hereby inform you that we no longer have the criminal report with its attachments." Now, tell the Trial Chamber, this Operation Septembar 1993, was it carried out by certain bodies in the army against civilian authorities? Was the building of the CSB Banja Luka surrounded? Did they go in? Was it a kind of military putsch?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And it's during these operations that certain documentation was removed from CSB Banja Luka, as this letter says?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, later on, there was also another Operation Hurricane in the same centre. Documents were removed, tampered with, manipulated. During this operation, too, there was a responsibility that a lot of documentation disappeared?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, certainly Defence counsel can -- this document has been admitted into evidence - and certainly Defence counsel can make whatever arguments they want at the end of the trial - but how can this witness comment on anything that happened to police files? Unless this witness has personal knowledge of this. Otherwise we're just simply reading a document to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In these conversations with your colleagues, with policemen, with prosecutors, did you discuss this, that papers were removed, that they were abused, that they were used in various scandals, et cetera? Tell us what you know.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of this Operation Septembar 93, and probably Hurricane as well, was, for these military structures, an element in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: A very specific question: Were documents removed?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were removed. And the purpose of Septembar 93 operation was to remove certain documentation. The army wanted to take some documents for their own reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. And as cherry on the top, the SFOR came later and removed even more documents. You were an eye-witness. And now, if we look at the prosecutions, when was it first -- when did it first become possible to collect evidence and documents in order to prosecute these crimes?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the full picture of the events during the war needed to be clear first, and it was towards the end of the war, or, rather, when peace was concluded in 1996 and onwards. That's also the time when military units were disbanded, police units, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's when the documents were gathered?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in the same period, Mr. Kovacevic, Stojan Zupljanin had held absolutely no post in the police?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the time, Stojan Zupljanin did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's time for break, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is coming back in, Mr. Pantelic tells me he's got about 15, 20 minutes left, and then I have, I think -- it's hard to say, but it could be upwards of 45 minutes of re-examination to cover the issues raised by Mr. Pantelic as well as by Mr. Zecevic. We have the witness on stand -- the next witness on stand by. Because he is a protected witness, I understand there's a 15, 20-minute time-period where the system has to be switched over. May that witness be excused for the day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to me the most practical course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, while we still have this document in front of us, which has a certain number of pages, let us use this opportunity to clarify an answer you gave to my colleague Mr. Olmsted. It's a minor thing, but it is my duty to clear up this issue with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's about page 14180 of the transcript; the date is 3rd of September, 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My learned colleague Mr. Olmsted asked you to interpret an Official Note made by Radovan Sukalo, who was a crime technician. This document was from 1992. And according to Mr. Sukalo, the investigative judge had not been at the on-site investigation at Koricanske Stijene. It may have been just an omission by my learned colleague Mr. Olmsted, who did not show to you page 35 of the document we have. It's in an Official Note made in 1999 by Mr. Zdenko Tesanovic. It is -- he's a anti-sabotage protection technician. And here it is stated that Jankovic, Jevto, who was the investigative judge of the basic court in Banja Luka who was there at the on-site investigation. Can you see that? It's somewhere in the middle of the page. It mentions inspector Markovic, and the on-site investigation was headed by Jevto Jankovic and so on.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We have some other examples. Buhovac is speaking about it. Also we can see it in the criminal report by the CSB Banja Luka, where this topic is discussed. So, first of all, do you remember this in your conversations with your boss, Mr. Pantic? Had he told you anything about a investigative judge being there on the on-site investigation site?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do remember that a commission was established, including a significant number of people, crime technicians, experts, and I think this commission also included my boss, Mr. Pantic, as well as Jevto Jankovic, the investigative judge. The commission was established for the very purpose of gaining insight into all the aspects, both legal and other aspects, of the case we're talking about. I believe they may have gone to the site, although I'm not sure about that. At least a part of the commission. Whether Mr. Jankovic went, I don't know. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's fine. My question was: If you remember, tell us. Now, the OTP investigator, when you were interviewed in 2003, showed you notes that accompanied the criminal report. And part of the notes were notes taken by two policemen from Knezevo who explained what they knew about the whole affair. You spoke about whether you received their notes and so forth. But what I'd like to clarify now is the following: Are you aware that, at a later stage, the investigative judge did take a statement from the two policemen, Milovanovic and Brkic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have no recollection of whether a statement was taken from them at a later stage. But, in any case, the investigative judge could have, as part of the on-site investigation, carry an interview with the two individuals about the statements they've given, especially in view of the fact that these two persons were reserve policemen from the Skender Vakuf area. So when I asked for or recommended certain investigative actions to be taken, when I asked the investigative judge to do that, for instance, to interview the victims, this investigative action was something that was delayed, and, therefore, Mr. Jankovic should have done it urgently. And as a part of these interviews, set of interviews, one could find, most probably, statements by these two policemen. But because of this possibility of delaying the statements by the victims, I assume the interrogation of the two policemen was not recommended either. But, in any case, Jevto Jankovic, the investigative judge, could have taken statements or could have interviewed the two policemen and notify me about these statements, even had he taken those statements in the area of Skender Vakuf. By taking the statements from the two policemen, he would have achieved something, but it wasn't done. Maybe because at the time the two of them were, for instance, somewhere on the front lines. So the recommendations related to what investigative actions needed to be taken would have been delayed because the victims needed to be interviewed immediately, without delay, and taken care of in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify the role of the judicial organs in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Pantelic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Ah, sorry, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we're trying to do now is clarify the role of the judicial organs in the case of Koricanske Stijene incidents. We have a memo that you forwarded to the investigative judge, Jevto Jankovic, a memo that has been discussed here. You've looked at the document. And the date of the document is September 1992. And in this document you are asking for eight persons, all eight persons, to be interviewed. You stated you were submitting relevant documentation for these persons. Then you attend the interviews on the 16th and the 17th of September, the office of the investigative judge. And then, finally, on the 24th -- on the 24th of September, the investigative judge - and this is ten days after you've sent a request - he then sends it back to you to make a decision. It must have been possible for the prosecutor's office to take some additional steps later on, to ask for some information, to carry out some activities in relation to this case; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We could have, in some form, at some later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And it is also a fact that the prosecutor's office did not take such actions, based on the documentation we have seen.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. The prosecutor's office did not do anything at a later stage. It did not try and hurry up the activities of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us state it like this: The prosecutor's office did not have an active role, did not exert pressure. We will not now go into why this could be only speculation, but that is the fact, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that the prosecutor's office does not have an active role at that stage. There are some actions that a prosecutor could have taken, but one cannot speak about some really active role that would have critically changed the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us now move to the case of -- we're talking about document 2D71. It's a document related to Vrbas case. In that case - and I'm asking you this question in your capacity of a prosecutor - for any investigative actions to even start, one must go into expertise of various aspects of the on-site investigation. All this needs to be done. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now why is that important? It is important to identify the victims and thereby set the framework, the time-frame work and other conditions; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And, of course, the investigation has to wait before the forensic results are obtained, and only then one can start looking for potential perpetrators; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, these victims got killed in front of the Manjaca Military Camp, and this camp was, as we know, disbanded at -- about that time, in November 1992, and it was impossible to find eye-witnesses or any witnesses of the crime, and I'm talking about victims here. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the evidence is not that the camp was disbanded in November of 1992. Just clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You can tell me whether -- was it in end of November, beginning of December?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it was in late 1992. I don't know precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Now let us look at this case file. Let's see what we have here. The case is still active. It has forensic foundations. So we have the foundations. What is necessary is to do -- to carry out further activities with a view to specify who the perpetrators were?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Whereas, in Koricanske Stijene case, you, the prosecutor, make a suggestion, recommendations for the activities that need to be done. Now, I don't see similar activity here in relation to the Vrbas River case. Mr. Kovacevic, let me give you options: I don't remember, you know, you don't know. What I'm saying here is there is no act from the public prosecutor sent to the investigative judge ordering him to take certain actions. Have you sent such a document to the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember sending such a document because the initial document relevant for Koricanske Stijene was related to the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I must specify that I'm discussing the River Vrbas case. There were eight victims found in the river who, according to some indications, were killed in front of Manjaca camp. So do you remember having sent an order to the investigative judge to take certain actions?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I don't remember having done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at page 19 of this document. The following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As can you see, on the 31st of December, 1992, the chief of department, Mr. Tegeltija, reports that through forensic investigation, some analysis was obtained, and here it is stated who the victims were: Mr. Crnalic, Krak, Bozic, and so on. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, can I.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In legal sense, in criminal investigation sense as well, what do we have here? At the end of 1992 -- I personally would like to see cases being completed in five days. However, we know how the real situation was. And what we have here is victims having been identified, and only then one can start looking for witnesses and so on. But the factual situation is the following: Nobody's left at Manjaca, so one cannot find them. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So, make it very -- let us make it very clear for the Trial Chamber. From the human point of view and professional, it would be terrible if we would know that something terrible had happened and nobody acts upon that, but here we can see that foundations were laid and then that -- those foundations help us come to justice. Now, justice comes slowly. But do we agree that the forensic and crime department police of the CSB Banja Luka actually did whatever they could under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, under the circumstances, I would agree with you. They did what they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, please, I'm coming to the conclusion of my cross-examination, and it is my duty to put to you the central question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need P1567, page ... page 53 of the Koricanske Stijene file.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Before I put to you this last question of mine, there's one procedural -- procedural issue we have to clarify, and it is the following: On the 29th of September, 2003, you gave a statement to the investigator of this Tribunal, Mr. Grady. On page 18 of the Serbian version, we can see you were shown two Official Notes relating to policemen from Knezevo. And then he quoted to you or told you the internal ERN number - for Milovanovic, it is number 0214-1510 - saying this for the transcript. We claim that in document P1567, so -- in that document, the statement that had been given by Milovanovic is marked as 0105-6486. The number I --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Before we confuse the witness with ERN numbers on documents, the ERNed -- a document could be ERNed more than once, and the English translations might have different ERNs depending on it. And I think that's a -- really a technical issue that this witness is not going to be able to comment on. But unless you can -- you can assert that he was shown a different document, I'm not sure this is going to get us anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It is absolutely not my intention. It's just my intention to clarify for the record, to have clean situation for -- for the further submissions. That's why. So I'm not challenging anything. Everything is fine. But I need to do that for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat. You were shown the statement that bears, as last three digits, 510, and in this case, in -- in the file, we have the other one with last three digits 486. Now, why am I insisting on that? Because, following the documents that follow -- that accompanied the criminal report, which are numbers 510 and then 511 and 512, all those documents were shown to you in 2003. From that, one can see that they were grouped together, these documents. Now, this other number that ends with 486, that system of numbering creates a confusion. Sow did gave -- you were interviewed by Paul Grady, and he did show you the two documents that we just discussed?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, but I said even then that I don't remember that these statements were in accompanying papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, I was just asking about numbers. You understand me about that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us move on. On the screen we can see a document from year 2000 issued by the district public prosecutor's office that was in charge of the case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And it's sent to the CSB Prijedor; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This document, and we will see that on the following page, was signed by Vlado Mandic, who was deputy public prosecutor, your colleague?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This Vlado Mandic, in year 2000, states in the final segment of the memo in the Serbian version, he is saying, We are convinced it is not correct that information cannot be obtained. We are aware that police members escorted the convoy --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please turn the page of the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then he says in some independent newspapers there are information being published, information is being gathered by the prosecutor. But you will agree with me that he is here, rather actively, addressing the CSB Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one can make such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, please, we heard about what the period was at the time. But as a professional and as a prosecutor, with all due respect to the then-prevailing circumstances, could you have done something more about this case? Could you be more active in the spirit of the standards that we can see from this letter? Can you tell me this as a human being.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, in hindsight, the circumstances were extremely difficult. And when one looks upon this entire event in that time-frame, I could have demonstrated a more active involvement in the sense that Mr. Mandic, the district deputy prosecutor, showed. But, to put it simply, I'm sorry, as -- as a human being, for not seeking more details. But it seems to me that nothing would have changed. The effect would perhaps be the same. But as I said, as a human being, I think that I omitted to cite certain things that I should have done that would be implied by the nature of things and which Mr. Mandic properly did in his letter. So I say I am sorry that I didn't write my letter in the same fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacevic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, I first want to talk about Koricanske Stijene and address some of the issues that was raised by Mr. Pantelic. Did the police ever inform you that the perpetrators of the crime at Koricanske Stijene were members of the military?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police never informed me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we looked through this case file which was transferred to the district prosecutor's office in 1999. Was this case ever transferred to the Military Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't transferred to the Military Prosecutor's Office, given that the military prosecutor offices were abolished. A reform of the military judiciary was carried out, and I think that they were abolished in 1998 as part of the overall reform and revamping of the judicial system in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, the military court and prosecutor's office existed from September 1992 through the remainder of the conflict. During that time-period, was this case ever transferred to the Military Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Until a case is transferred from the civilian prosecutor's office to the Military's Prosecutor's Office, it remains a case within your jurisdiction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for this particular crime that the perpetrators were reported for, there was no dispute that the civilian prosecutor was responsible in terms of dealing with the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, I know you've probably grown tired of all our hypothetical questions, but I do want to ask a couple. And perhaps to clarify some matters. I want you to -- you to think of this scenario: We have a civilian police officer who commits a crime of murder, for instance, but he's a civilian police officer. There's no question that he is civilian. Now, after he commits that murder, a few weeks later, he is temporarily assigned to a war unit along the front lines. Now, after his wartime assignment, he returns to his civilian police responsibilities. When he returns to his civilian life, can you, as a civilian prosecutor, prosecute him for that murder that he committed before he went to the front lines?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we need to have precise information relating to this hypothetical career moves, let's put it that way, that, first, he was a civilian, then he joined an army unit, then he left the army unit. What I want to say is we need to have this exact information in order to be able to establish who is responsible for conducting prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And assume, for purposes of my hypothetical, that the information is exact. So this is in fact what is determined: That he was civilian when he committed the crime; then he just temporarily was assigned to the front lines; and then he came back and he is a civilian again. Can the civilian prosecutor's office then prosecute him for that murder he committed while he was a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is such a possibility. But, as I said, this information is crucial, and they have to be relevant and verified; that is to say, that he was seconded to the army in a lawful way, that he was discharged from the army, in a lawful way, et cetera. This is key information that would determine what the answer to your hypothetical question would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, let's assume that it's determined that he was civilian. Now, he's gone off to the front lines for a few weeks. In the meantime, can the civilian prosecutor's office open an investigation against this person for that civilian crime? Is there anything that stops the civilian prosecutor from doing that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has to have information that at the time of the commission of the crime this particular individual was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, let's leave that hypothetical aside. I want to you give a different hypothetical now. We have a civilian police officer who commits, again, a murder as a civilian. A few weeks later, he joins the military, and he stays with the military. It's not temporary; he stays with the military. Who has jurisdiction to prosecute him for the crime he committed while he was a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me clarify one thing: The jurisdiction for conducting proceedings against civilian - and it's absolutely clear to everyone - is civilian judiciary. However, when one changes one's status, that is to say, if somebody joined a military unit and he is needed there, the civilian judiciary cannot have any jurisdiction over a member of military. It cannot address his command or whoever with a request to discharge this soldier so that he can be arrested and placed in custody. That would be possible only if the security organs, or, rather, the military police, establishes this fact and deals with the whole case, operationally and in the sense of criminal investigation, and then forward it to the Military Prosecutor's Office. If the military prosecutor determines that at the time of the commission of crime he was a civilian, in the army there's a variety of ways to strip someone of his status of a member of the military personnel, and, thereafter, this case is referred to the civilian judiciary for further processing. First of all, to the court; and then to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the last word.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: First to the court and then to the ...? We didn't catch the end.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either to the court, if he is in detention, because of the deadline set down by the law; and, if, in the meantime, his status is being resolved and he is no longer a soldier, he is placed in civilian detention and he comes under the jurisdiction of the investigating judge. At that point, the civilian prosecutor becomes involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in this hypothetical, the police officer committed the crime while he was a civilian. Now he's -- in a military unit. Whose responsibility is it to inform the military prosecutor that they have a criminal amongst their ranks?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a difficult question. First of all, such an individual cannot join any army unit on their own initiative, whether he be a criminal or not a criminal. No one can join the army on their own initiative. They have to have certain status, whether they have work obligation, whether they were a reserve police officer, et cetera. So there is an established procedure for people to be assigned to war units and thereby change their status. What was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine. Let's assume that the military doesn't know that this person who's now joined the military had committed a crime while they were a civilian, a serious crime like a murder. So they have now this murderer amongst their ranks, but they don't know it. Whose responsibility is it to inform the military prosecutor that this -- this civilian had committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I think we are going --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Kovacevic, please. I think we are going a bit too far here. I mean, at the moment when these gentlemen were transferred or resubordinated from the police to the army there was at the most, perhaps, a suspicion, and there was certainly no conviction for having committed the crime at this point. And I just wonder if I may address your line of questioning in general, how useful it is to pursue this matter. Because I think the end result was, and we know this as a fact now, that the case was eventually assumed by the public prosecutor. So if ever the military prosecutor had any action in this case, it was very short and very brief; and the case, as I said, ended up with the public prosecutor, so -- and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I see your point, and I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just one more series of questions with regard to the investigation into the Koricanske Stijene matter. And I want you to base this on your experience as a prosecutor. As a prosecutor, who would you have expected the police to interview to find more evidence about this crime? We've talked -- we already know that they interviewed the victims. But who else?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Potential suspects and eye-witnesses. And other witnesses, potential witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What about members of the police leadership at SJB Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty of the SJB Prijedor, given that these individuals were from their territory, was to undertake all measures with a view to detecting and establishing the identity of the perpetrators, of questioning them, arresting them under the regulations then in force, and bringing them into custody, bringing them then before the investigating judge. And the rest was supposed to be taken care of by the prosecutor and the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to move on to another topic entirely. Now, on Friday, you were asked a number of questions by Mr. Zecevic regarding the functioning of the military courts and the prosecutor's office in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen Exhibit 1D367.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is a report by the 1st Krajina Corps Military Prosecutor's Office, dated 19 September 1992. And if we can turn to page 2 of both the B/C/S and the English, Mr. Zecevic drew your attention to the second paragraph under Roman numeral II, entitled: "Review of Crime Trends," where it says that a few thousand cases were currently being resolved. To put that into some context, I would like to draw your attention to what is written a few paragraphs below that, where it states: "The largest number of cases related to the avoidance of military service described under Article 217 of the SFRY Criminal Code and other crimes against armed forces." Mr. Kovacevic, do you recall that desertion was a major issue for the military in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know -- Your Honours, with all due respect, I don't see how does this come out of my cross-examination. I posed a very specific question concerning this -- this statistical data and never, ever mentioned some other crimes. I concentrated on what is relevant in this case, and I would kindly ask that Mr. Olmsted be instructed accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to respond, but could we ask the witness to take off his headphones before I give you an argument on why this is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Does he speak English?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think very little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In your view, that would be sufficient; he doesn't have to be escorted from the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, the Defence argument -- and perhaps Mr. Zecevic can explain to me if I get it wrong, but as I understand it the Defence's argument in this case is that the crimes charged in our indictment were crimes that fell within the jurisdiction of the military courts and then that the military courts were inundated with these cases and unable to process them. Now, the Prosecution's position is that crimes charged in the indictment are largely cases that fall within the civilian jurisdiction. And at any rate, the military courts were not inundated with criminal reports of the crimes that we charge in the indictment but, rather, were processing ordinary or typical crimes that you would expect them to be prosecuting in times where they have military actions, which would include these particular types of crimes, crimes involving a failure to report to military duty or desertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, I -- I clearly showed to the -- to the witness, again, what is relevant, that the military judicial -- judicial organs were involved and were actually conducting the -- or processing the cases of the -- of the war crimes and crimes against humanity. Therefore, those are the questions. I didn't went [sic] any further than that. Now, if Mr. Olmsted wants to show what else were the military organs doing, I don't see how is that relevant. That was the point of my objection, Your Honours, at this very beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As I understand Mr. Olmsted's response, it is in the context of the Prosecution's case that this is being asked -- that -- that the question is being asked. And this document appears to specifically explain what the military courts were primarily concerned with. So it appears to me that the question is permissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The witness can put back on his headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Mr. Kovacevic. Again, I want to refer you to the paragraph which points out that the largest number of cases relates to the avoidance of military service under Article 217 of the Criminal Code. Do you recall that desertion was a major issue for the military in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, were you aware that a significant portion of the criminal cases processed by the Military Prosecutor's Office in 1992 and beyond pertained to the crime of desertion?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose so. I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zecevic also asked you a number of questions regarding the military court's jurisdiction over war crimes, or at least war-crime cases. Are you aware of any cases brought, in 1992 or 1993, against Serb civilians for committing war crimes against non-Serb civilians, regardless of whether it was before a military court or a civilian court or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In practical terms, if, in 1992, the police reported to your office a crime committed by a Serb civilian that had the elements of a war crime or crime against humanity, what would your office have done with it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I already said that if that was a case of aggravated murder, according to Article 362, paragraph 5, the police in charge should file a criminal report. This does not have to be only the police. A state organ can file such a report as well, provided they have this kind of information. Then, through intelligence work on the ground with the assistance of police, we established the elements relevant for the criminal report. And I think that would be the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In 1992, did you ever receive any instructions from Prosecutor Pantic on how to process criminal reports charging crimes against humanity or war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't receive any special instructions and guide-lines because, at the time, it went without saying that for this type of crimes the military judiciary would have jurisdiction, for the crimes committed against civilian population and international law. So everybody understood that, should such incident happen, these cases would be processed by the military judiciary. And I think that even at one of our staff meetings - I'm not sure - we discussed, to a certain extent, this issue of jurisdiction and that it was established then that it would undoubtedly be the military jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall, was that meeting in 1992, 1993, or can you give us any idea?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but it was at the beginning of my term of office. 1993, perhaps. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic showed you four criminal reports against unknown perpetrators for Article 172, causing general danger crimes against non-Serb victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: For the record, these cases have been assigned exhibit numbers 1D371, 1D372, and 1D373, and 1D374.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in order to save time, I want to hand you hard copies of these four exhibits. Now, keep them in order because that's the order I want to discuss them in. And I first want you to take a look at the one that's on top. One -- Exhibit 1D374. And do you notice that it has a K-U or KU entry number 3566/92? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: /92, yeah, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if you can look at, now, 1D372, we see that it has a KU entry number of 3567/92.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can have P1574 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is the Banja Luka Basic Prosecutor's Office KTN log-book for 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 29. Are we on page 29? It was too small for me to see. Yes. Okay. And if we can now -- if we can go look -- zoom in to entries 2346 and 2347. They're on the right-hand page, I think a little bit towards the bottom. We need to zoom in a little bit more because it's quite small on the screen. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that -- we see the two KU entry numbers for these two unknown perpetrator cases in the third column, is that correct, under entries 2346 and 2347?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we can just scroll up really quickly to show the heading of column 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, we see in column 9 -- first of all, before we do, we see, in the ninth column, we see the date -- dates 24 September 1992 and 21 September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could just scroll up so he can see the heading for column number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you confirm that those are the dates that the prosecutor's office sent requests to the police to collect needed information, under column 9?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it says here - and it does - that this request was sent to the police, then it must have been sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, column 16 - and we talked a little bit about this during your examination - is where the name of the perpetrator, if identified by the police, would be recorded along with the KT entry number to which the case was transferred; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we look at the first entry, 2346, we don't see anything written in column 16. So does this mean that this case remained an unidentified perpetrator case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. That means the perpetrator was not detected.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the entry for 2347, we see, in column 16, a date which appears to be the 29th of May, 2000, and then something written underneath it. Can you tell us what happened to this particular case?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The case was sent to the district prosecutor's office in Banja Luka in May 2000 because jurisdiction had changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now I want you to look at Exhibit 1D371. And if you can see that it has -- yes, that's the third one in your pile. You can see that it was a KU entry number of 3709/92.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can turn -- please turn to page 35 of the KTN log-book. And if we can -- yes, we don't need to call up the criminal report because he has that in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in that case, I would need the tab number, please, from my list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise, I don't have that. You admitted it into evidence. It's 1D371, admitted. This is not ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, 371.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to page 35 of the KTN log-book, which is P1574. And if this is page 35, if we can go to the left-hand page and look at entry 2454.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we can see in column 3 it has the KU entry number 3709/92 written in it. Now, according to this entry, was the perpetrator in this case ever identified by the police?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see further in the register. Something is missing. It's very close up. We need to zoom out a little. And now zoom back in again, please, a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now you can see the whole entry -- or the whole line for the entry. Now --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something is missing like -- we need to see the end of the last page. There's nothing there. All right. No? So it's not there. There is no entry that the perpetrator was identified. It's not entered. That means he was not identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Finally, if we can look at Exhibit 1D373.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And while you're looking at that, if we can turn to page 44 of the log-book. And this is the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you look at Exhibit 1D373, we can see that it has a KU entry number of 3925/92.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But, again, if we can stay -- there seems to be miscommunication between me and -- I want to keep on the log-book. If we can turn to the log-book and turn to page 44 of the log-book. The witness has the criminal report in front of him, so we don't need to call it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, but I don't seem to understand the relevance of this redirect examination. Because if my learned friend wants to show that it's -- that these -- that these criminal complaints have been recorded with the Office of the Prosecutor, we're going to stipulate that. I don't -- if, however, the idea is that -- to show that there is un -- that the -- that the perpetrators were not found, I don't -- it's probably me, I didn't understand that the that the -- that the OTP case was -- actually had anything to do with the results of the work of the police in 1992. If we are talking about the -- the statistics of the -- or the results of the work of the -- of the -- of the police in 1992, then, perhaps this would be relevant, but I don't think that that was the -- that is the Prosecutor's case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Zecevic tendered through this witness over the Prosecution's objection these criminal reports that this witness knew nothing or very little about. I want the witness to help us figure out what happened to these cases through a document that he is familiar with, which is this KTN log-book. I can explain further, but I need to ask that the witness's headphones be removed, and I can explain the relevance in the context of the entire case. And, at any rate, this is my -- this is the last entry I want to go through because it was the last criminal report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And you do appreciate that it's time to take the adjournment?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. And I think we can do this in one minute, if I'm allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed. One minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can please zoom in -- again, please take the criminal report off the screen and just focus in on the log-book. And if we can please look at entry number 3925. We have to be on page 44. And if this is page 44, if we can just -- it's going to be on the left-hand page, and it's 3925. Is this page 44? This is it not page 44. This is page 44? Then, Your Honours, I will finish up with this one, I think, at the beginning of next session. And work out the technical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the witness has to return tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I have, I think, about 20 more minutes, maybe less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we take the -- we rise now and take the adjournment to -- I believe we're in Courtroom I tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
